summary: Specifies the 5G Wireless Wireline Convergence User Plane Encapsulation (5WE), used between 5G residential gateways and the 5G Access Gateway Function. It multiplexes traffic of several PDU sessions within a VLAN-delineated circuit and carries 5G QoS information.

plainLanguage.summary: A way of packing several phone-network connections into one home line while keeping labels visible.

questions: how is 5g traffic carried over fixed access
subtitle: Encapsulation for 5G residential gateway traffic over wireline networks.

tldr.problem: 5G networks need to carry user traffic between residential gateways and access functions over existing wireline networks, while supporting multiple connections and quality-of-service information.
tldr.mechanism: 5WE encapsulates multiple PDU sessions in a VLAN circuit using a header similar to PPPoE, carrying per-packet QoS information and efficient encoding.
tldr.outcome: Wireline access networks can carry 5G traffic using existing equipment that understands PPPoE-like headers without modification.

today: RFC 8822 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated, so 5WE remains the specified encapsulation for 5G user plane traffic over wireline access networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
5G Wireless Wireline Convergence User Plane Encapsulation (5WE) allows wireline networks to carry user data for 5G systems. It is used between 5G residential gateways and the 5G Access Gateway Function across deployed broadband networks.

The protocol multiplexes traffic from multiple 5G connections (PDU sessions) over a single VLAN-identified circuit. It achieves this by reusing the structure of the PPPoE header but with fields repurposed for 5G, allowing existing equipment in the data path to identify and inspect packets without modification.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireline networks (like cable and DSL) can now carry phone-network traffic for 5G homes. 5WE packs multiple connections into one circuit using a familiar packet format.

sections.title: Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
A 5WE packet begins with a 6-byte header followed by a 2-byte protocol type identifier. The header contains:

  • VER (version): Set to 2 to distinguish 5WE from PPPoE version 1.
  • TYPE: Set to 1 for data packets.
  • QFI (QoS Flow Identifier): Encodes the 3GPP 5G QoS Flow Identifier to map quality-of-service classes.
  • R (Reflective QoS Indication): One bit set by the network for downstream traffic to indicate QoS feedback.
  • SESSION_ID: A 16-bit identifier distinguishing different PDU sessions in the multiplex. The value 0xffff is reserved.
  • LENGTH: The size of the payload in bytes.
  • PROTOCOL ID: Identifies the payload type using PPP protocol numbers. Valid values are 0x0021 (IPv4), 0x0031 (Ethernet), and 0x0057 (IPv6).

The maximum payload for each protocol type depends on the underlying VLAN circuit, typically 1500 bytes or less.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is like an address label: it says which connection this packet belongs to, what quality it should get, and what kind of data it contains.

sections.title: Session Identification and Multiplexing
sections.content:
Multiple PDU sessions are distinguished by their SESSION_ID value within a single VLAN-delineated circuit. Each session carries one type of 5G traffic with its own QoS requirements.

When equipment processes 5WE frames, it checks the version field first. If the version is 1, it processes the frame as PPPoE; if version is 2, it processes it as 5WE. Frames with unrecognized session IDs MUST be silently discarded. This ensures backward compatibility with deployed PPPoE equipment that ignores the VER, TYPE, and CODE fields.

The QFI field allows the network to communicate per-packet QoS requirements, enabling equipment to apply appropriate quality-of-service treatments such as priority scheduling or rate limiting.
sections.plainLanguage: Each connection gets its own ID number so packets don't get mixed up. The network can also label each packet with its priority level.

sections.title: Deployment and Compatibility
sections.content:
5WE is designed for environments where PPPoE is already deployed, such as broadband access networks using DSLAMs (Digital Subscriber Loop Access Multiplexers) and OLTs (Optical Line Terminations). These devices currently inspect packets with Ethertype 0x8864 to identify PPPoE and other protocols for enhanced QoS, access control, and monitoring.

By using the same Ethertype and maintaining field offsets compatible with PPPoE, 5WE allows these legacy devices to continue their inspections without modification. The redefinition of unused fields (VER, TYPE, and CODE) enables 5WE to implement 5G-specific functionality while preserving compatibility.

5WE is not suitable for use over the public Internet or untrusted networks, as it relies on trusted non-3GPP access without ciphering.
sections.plainLanguage: The equipment in the network doesn't need to be changed; it already knows how to handle 5WE because it looks similar to an older protocol called PPPoE.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
5G NAS procedures employed for session life-cycle maintenance provide ciphering and integrity protection, which is more secure than legacy PPPoE session establishment against on-path attackers. The design of 5WE does not circumvent existing anti-spoofing and security procedures in deployed equipment.

5WE-encapsulated traffic is used on what the 5G Core considers trusted non-3GPP interfaces, so it does not use additional ciphering. 5WE is not suitable for deployment over untrusted interfaces or public networks without additional security measures.
sections.plainLanguage: 5WE relies on the 5G system's own security to protect the connection, so it doesn't add its own encryption. It's only meant for trusted wireline networks, not the open Internet.
